intro.html: Every contest, court case and news story raises the same question: is the judgment fair? This topic gives you the words for a fair judge and for the things that spoil fairness, from a small leaning to a sour, suspicious eye.

Fair: impartial (takes no side), disinterested (has nothing to gain), objective (sticks to facts), equitable (fair to all), dispassionate (calm, not swayed by feelings). Unfair or shaky: subjective (based on personal taste), bias (a leaning), prejudice (judging before knowing), arbitrary (based on whim), jaundiced (soured by bitterness).
Watch for one famous trap: disinterested does not mean bored. It means having no personal stake, which is exactly what you want in a referee.

words.def: treating all sides equally; not taking sides
words.ex: A good referee stays {impartial}, even when her hometown team is playing.
words.ctx: Because the judge had never met either family, she could be {impartial}, weighing only the facts each side presented.
words.etym: From im- (not) + partial, “favoring one part or side.”

mn.cue: IM-PARTIAL: not PARTIAL to either side
mn.text: Nana Lou judges the pie contest wearing a blindfold, so she can’t favor her own grandson’s pie: she is {impartial}.

scene.alt: A grandmother in a blindfold tastes two pies while two children wait nervously.

words.def: having nothing to gain or lose, and so able to judge fairly
words.ex: We asked a {disinterested} neighbor to settle the argument, since she had no stake in it.
words.ctx: The two bakeries agreed to let a {disinterested} expert choose the best bread; because she would earn nothing either way, both trusted her verdict.
words.etym: From dis- (not) + interested, in its old sense of “having a stake or a share.”
words.note: Careful: disinterested is not uninterested (bored). Many people now use it to mean bored, but careful writers and test makers keep the two apart. A disinterested judge is a fair one.

mn.cue: no INTEREST (no stake) in who wins
mn.text: Professor Edwin judges the pet show because he owns no pets: he gains nothing whoever wins. He is {disinterested}.

scene.alt: An old professor with no pets of his own judges a dog and a cat at a pet show.

words.def: based on facts rather than personal feelings
words.ex: A thermometer gives an {objective} reading of the temperature.
words.ctx: Reviewers argue about whether the movie is good, but its length is an {objective} fact: it runs exactly two hours and ten minutes.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin objectivus, from objectum, “a thing put before the mind”: ob- (before) + jacere (to throw).

mn.text: Dev and Jonah argue about whose fish is bigger, so Ada simply measures each one with a ruler: the answer is {objective}.

scene.alt: A woman settles an argument by measuring a fish with a ruler.

words.def: based on personal feelings, tastes or opinions
words.ex: Whether a song is beautiful is partly a {subjective} question.
words.ctx: The judges tried to follow clear rules, but scoring a painting is partly {subjective}: one judge loved its bold colors while another found them far too loud.
words.etym: From Latin subjectivus, from subicere (to place under): sub- (under) + jacere (to throw).

mn.cue: depends on the SUBJECT: the person
mn.text: Sami tastes the soup and gasps “Too spicy!”; Tia tastes the same soup and says “Not spicy enough!” Spiciness here is {subjective}.

scene.alt: Two people taste the same soup; one finds it far too spicy and the other too mild.

words.def: a leaning for or against someone that gets in the way of fair judgment
words.ex: The coach admitted a {bias} toward players who showed up early.
words.ctx: Because the reviewer’s brother had made the film, readers suspected {bias} in her glowing review rather than fair judgment.

mn.cue: BY US: he always picks ours
mn.text: In the art contest, Grandpa always picks the drawings made by us, his grandkids, whatever they look like: that is {bias}.

labels.text: BY US: he picks his own

scene.alt: A grandfather picks his grandson’s scribble as the winner while a girl with a fine painting looks sad.

words.def: an opinion formed before knowing the facts, usually an unfair one
words.ex: Lila tried to read the new book without {prejudice}, even though she had disliked the author’s first one.
words.ctx: The coach admitted his {prejudice} against short players, formed before he had seen them play, until a five-foot guard led the team in steals.
words.etym: From Latin praejudicium, “a judgment in advance”: prae- (before) + judicium (judgment).

mn.text: Dev decides he hates mushrooms before he has tasted a single bite: “Yuck!” He is judging ahead of time, out of {prejudice}.

scene.alt: A teen crosses his arms and says “Yuck!” at a plate of mushrooms he has never tasted.

words.def: based on whim or chance rather than on reason
words.ex: The order of the names on the list was {arbitrary}; it meant nothing at all.
words.ctx: Students complained that the new dress code was {arbitrary}: no one could explain why green socks were allowed but blue ones were not.
words.etym: From Latin arbitrarius, “depending on a judge’s choice,” from arbiter (judge).

mn.cue: the king rolls the dice: no reason at all
mn.text: King Victor rolls dice to decide each new rule: “Tuesday: no hats!” His rules are {arbitrary}.

scene.alt: A king tosses dice to make up a silly rule while a man in a hat scratches his head.

words.def: fair and just to everyone involved
words.ex: The sisters worked out an {equitable} plan for sharing the bike.
words.ctx: The new carpool schedule was more {equitable} than the old one; instead of the same two families always driving, every family took a turn.
words.etym: From French équitable, from équité (fairness), from Latin aequitas, from aequus (equal, fair).

mn.cue: EQUI-TABLE: EQUAL shares at the TABLE
mn.text: Nell cuts the pizza into equal slices so everyone at the table gets the same: her way of sharing is {equitable}.

scene.alt: A woman shares a pizza in equal slices among the children at the table.

words.def: calm and fair; not swayed by strong feelings
words.ex: The scientist gave a {dispassionate} report of the results, neither cheering nor complaining.
words.ctx: While the fans screamed and argued, the referee remained {dispassionate}, calmly reviewing the replay before making her call.

mn.cue: DIS-PASSION: no PASSION, just a calm call
mn.text: The fans shout and stamp, but the referee calmly checks the line and makes her call: she is {dispassionate}.

scene.alt: A calm referee makes a call while one fan rages and another cheers.

words.def: soured by bitterness, envy or distrust
words.ex: After losing money once, Uncle Victor took a {jaundiced} view of every bargain.
words.ctx: Years of broken promises had given the villagers a {jaundiced} view of the bridge plan; they assumed it would never be finished, whatever the builders said.
words.etym: From jaundice, an illness that yellows the skin; people once believed it made everything look yellow to the sufferer, so a jaundiced eye sees the world in a sour light.

mn.text: Ivy offers Uncle Victor a free cookie, but he squints through his old yellow glasses: “What’s the catch?” His view of everything is {jaundiced}.

scene.alt: A girl offers a free cookie, and a man in yellowish goggles crosses his arms, suspicious.

head: fair
unfair or shaky
rows: bias: a leaning toward one side
after.cap: A fair judge and the things that get in the way.

after.html: disinterested = having no personal stake, so fair. uninterested = not interested, bored. “The disinterested judge listened closely” is high praise; “the uninterested judge yawned” is not.
Subjective is not always bad. Taste in music is subjective, and that is fine. It becomes a problem only when a judgment that should rest on facts rests on feelings instead.

items.q: The judge owns neither of the companies in the case and will gain nothing whoever wins. The judge is…
items.why: Having nothing to gain makes the judge disinterested: able to be fair. Uninterested would mean bored.

items.q: True or false: a disinterested referee is one who is bored by the game.
items.why: False. A disinterested referee has no stake in who wins. A bored referee is uninterested.

choices: The bridge is the prettiest in the state.
The bridge is boring to look at.
items.why: A length can be measured and checked, so it is objective. Prettiest and boring are matters of taste: subjective.

items.q: The principal banned green backpacks but allowed blue ones, and gave no reason at all. The rule was…
items.why: A rule based on whim, with no reason behind it, is arbitrary.
